Chapter 10. Coming Home: What Remains After the Journey.
Sooner or later, every road trip has to end. You turn your car back toward home, watching the miles slip away in the rearview mirror, and those familiar sights start popping up again. There’s a relief in that—coming home always feels good. But there’s also a bit of sadness, isn’t there? The adventure’s behind you now, and the big questions you picked up along the way haven’t all been answered.
Back in the city, life picks up right where you left it. The job calls, the bills arrive, and those daily routines you almost forgot about, they’re right there waiting. But you know something’s shifted. You’re carrying the journey with you now—a new perspective, a deeper sense of what really matters. Think about it: the musicians who’ve passed on, the stories you heard, the songs that played as you drove. They’re all woven into the bigger story of your life, a story that’s still unfolding.
When old friends ask about your trip, they want to know what you discovered out there. But how do you explain it? The truth is, it wasn’t about finding neat answers. It was about learning to live with the questions. Realizing that everyone’s out there searching for meaning, and that we all have our own ghosts we carry.
Picture this: one night, you’re sitting with a friend, sharing a drink, letting an old record spin. Suddenly, the music feels totally different. There’s a richness to it now, a complexity—like it’s holding all the things you’ve lost and all the things you’ve found. There’s comfort in that. Because you realize the journey didn’t really end when you pulled into your driveway. Every day, you get another chance to keep searching, to keep listening, to keep living.
Most of us don’t even notice how much we’ve changed until we look back. But on the road, with nothing but time and music for company, the truth stands out: the stories we tell about death are really stories about life. About what it means to love, to lose, and to keep moving forward.
